subChunks.title: HTTP Methods, Status Codes & REST Principles
subChunks.hookHtml: Most of the software you will build as a Java engineer will talk to other systems over the network. REST is the architectural style that governs how those conversations happen. Understanding it is not optional — it is foundational.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is REST?

REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for building APIs over HTTP. A RESTful API exposes resources (nouns) at URLs and uses HTTP methods (verbs) to describe actions on them.

HTTP Methods

MethodActionSafe?Idempotent?
GETRetrieve a resource✅ Yes✅ Yes
POSTCreate a new resource❌ No❌ No
PUTReplace a resource entirely❌ No✅ Yes
PATCHPartially update a resource❌ NoDepends
DELETERemove a resource❌ No✅ Yes

Safe: does not modify data. Idempotent: calling it multiple times has the same effect as calling it once.

HTTP Status Codes

  • 2xx — Success: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
  • 3xx — Redirect: 301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified
  • 4xx — Client Error: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorised, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Entity
  • 5xx — Server Error: 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable

RESTful URL Design

GET    /api/spells          → list all spells
POST   /api/spells          → create a new spell
GET    /api/spells/{id}     → get one spell
PUT    /api/spells/{id}     → replace a spell
PATCH  /api/spells/{id}     → partially update a spell
DELETE /api/spells/{id}     → delete a spell

// Nested resources:
GET    /api/mages/{id}/spells  → spells assigned to a mage

REST Constraints

  1. Stateless: each request contains all information the server needs; no session state stored server-side
  2. Uniform interface: resources identified by URLs; standard methods; self-descriptive messages
  3. Client-server separation: frontend and backend are independent and communicate only through the API
  4. Cacheable: GET responses should indicate whether they can be cached

storyBeats.text: The Academy's inter-tower communication network carries thousands of requests per second — spell lookups, enrolment confirmations, mana transfers. All of it travels as structured HTTP requests following a single architectural convention.

storyBeats.speaker: Network Mage Aris
storyBeats.text: REST is not a protocol — it's a set of conventions. Resources are nouns in the URL. HTTP methods are the verbs. GET reads, never writes. POST creates. PUT replaces. DELETE removes. The URL tells you what you're acting on; the method tells you what you're doing to it.

storyBeats.speaker: RESTful API for the spell registry
storyBeats.text:
GET    /api/spells          → 200 OK + JSON array of spells
POST   /api/spells          → 201 Created + new spell JSON
GET    /api/spells/42       → 200 OK + spell #42, or 404 Not Found
DELETE /api/spells/42       → 204 No Content (success, nothing to return)

storyBeats.speaker: Network Mage Aris
storyBeats.text: Status codes are part of the contract. 200 is success. 201 is created. 400 means your request is malformed — your fault. 401 means you are not authenticated. 403 means you are authenticated but not authorised. 404 means the resource does not exist. 500 means we broke something on the server — never let this escape to a client without a clean message.

storyBeats.speaker: Network Mage Aris
storyBeats.text: The most important REST constraint: stateless. Every request must contain everything the server needs. No server-side session storing 'which mage is logged in'. The authentication token travels in the request header every time.

learningObjectives: Match each HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) to its purpose and idempotency
Identify the correct HTTP status code for a given scenario
Design RESTful URLs for a simple resource hierarchy
Explain the stateless constraint and why it matters for scalability
commonMistakes: Using GET for operations that modify state — GET must be safe and idempotent
Returning 200 for all responses, including errors — clients cannot distinguish success from failure
Putting verbs in URLs (e.g. /api/deleteSpell) — REST uses HTTP methods as verbs, not URL segments
Confusing 401 Unauthorised (not authenticated) with 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not authorised)
assessmentCriteria: Can design a complete set of REST endpoints for a resource with correct methods and URL patterns
Can state the correct status code for: resource not found, validation error, successful creation, no content, server error
Can explain what 'idempotent' means and give examples of idempotent and non-idempotent methods
Can explain why REST's stateless constraint makes horizontal scaling easier
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain REST to a colleague who only knows how to write desktop applications. What is a resource? What are the HTTP methods and what do they do? Why does 'stateless' matter?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Design the REST API for the Academy's Spell Registry:

  1. Write out the full set of endpoints (method + URL) for CRUD on spells
  2. For each scenario below, state the correct HTTP status code and a one-line explanation:
    - A client requests spell ID 9999 which does not exist
    - A client sends a POST with a missing required field
    - A client successfully creates a new spell
    - The server crashes while processing a request
    - A client successfully deletes a spell
  3. A client sends: POST /api/spells/delete/42. What is wrong with this URL, and what should it be?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Spell Registry endpoints:
   GET    /api/spells          → list all spells
   POST   /api/spells          → create a spell
   GET    /api/spells/{id}     → get one spell
   PUT    /api/spells/{id}     → replace a spell
   PATCH  /api/spells/{id}     → partial update
   DELETE /api/spells/{id}     → delete a spell

2. Status codes:
   - Spell not found            → 404 Not Found
   - Missing required field     → 400 Bad Request (or 422 Unprocessable Entity)
   - Spell created successfully → 201 Created
   - Server crash               → 500 Internal Server Error
   - Spell deleted              → 204 No Content

3. Problem: the verb 'delete' is in the URL — REST uses HTTP methods as verbs.
   Correct: DELETE /api/spells/42
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
You are designing a REST API for a blog platform with Posts and Comments. A Post has a title, body, and author. A Comment belongs to a Post and has a body and commenter name.

Write: (a) all REST endpoints for Posts and for Comments nested under a Post. (b) The status code the server should return for each: a request to get a post that exists, creating a comment successfully, deleting a comment that doesn't exist, a request without authentication to create a post. (c) One sentence explaining why POST /api/posts is NOT idempotent.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) Post endpoints:
  GET    /api/posts             → list all posts
  POST   /api/posts             → create post
  GET    /api/posts/{id}        → get post
  PUT    /api/posts/{id}        → replace post
  DELETE /api/posts/{id}        → delete post

  Comment endpoints (nested):
  GET    /api/posts/{id}/comments         → list comments for post
  POST   /api/posts/{id}/comments         → add comment to post
  DELETE /api/posts/{id}/comments/{cid}   → remove a comment

(b) Status codes:
  Get existing post          → 200 OK
  Comment created            → 201 Created
  Delete non-existent comment → 404 Not Found
  Unauthenticated POST       → 401 Unauthorised

(c) POST /api/posts is not idempotent because each call creates a new post — calling it 3 times creates 3 posts, not the same post 3 times.

questions.questionHtml: A REST API endpoint successfully creates a new resource. Which status code should it return?
questions.explanationHtml: 201 Created indicates that the request succeeded and a new resource was created. The response typically includes a Location header pointing to the new resource's URL and the created resource in the body.

questions.questionHtml: A REST API that stores session state on the server (e.g. 'which user is logged in') is fully RESTful.
questions.explanationHtml: REST's stateless constraint requires that each request contain all information needed to process it. Server-side session state violates this — if the server stores who is logged in, requests from the same client must hit the same server, preventing horizontal scaling.

questions.questionHtml: A user is authenticated but tries to access an admin endpoint they are not allowed to use. Which status code is correct?
questions.explanationHtml: 401 means the client is not authenticated (no valid credentials). 403 means the client IS authenticated but lacks the permission for this action. Some APIs return 404 instead of 403 to avoid revealing that the resource exists, but 403 is semantically correct.

subChunks.title: Calling REST APIs with Java's HttpClient
subChunks.hookHtml: Knowing the theory of REST is half the job. The other half is writing the code that actually makes HTTP requests. Since Java 11, the standard library includes HttpClient — a modern, fluent API for calling REST endpoints.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
java.net.http.HttpClient (Java 11+)

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse.BodyHandlers;

// Build a client (reusable)
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient();

// Build a GET request
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.example.com/spells"))
    .header("Accept", "application/json")
    .GET()
    .build();

// Send synchronously
HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
System.out.println(response.statusCode()); // 200
System.out.println(response.body());       // JSON string

POST with a JSON Body

String json = "{\"name\":\"Frostbolt\",\"damage\":120}";

HttpRequest post = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.example.com/spells"))
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(json))
    .build();

HttpResponse<String> res = client.send(post, BodyHandlers.ofString());
System.out.println(res.statusCode()); // 201

Handling the Response

if (response.statusCode() == 200) {
    // parse body
} else if (response.statusCode() == 404) {
    System.out.println("Not found");
} else {
    throw new RuntimeException("API error: " + response.statusCode());
}

Async Request

client.sendAsync(request, BodyHandlers.ofString())
      .thenApply(HttpResponse::body)
      .thenAccept(System.out::println);
// Non-blocking — returns immediately, processes when ready

storyBeats.text: The Academy's cross-tower communication spell has been replaced with a Java client. Junior engineers are expected to call external registries, look up spell databases, and post enrolment confirmations — all via HTTP.

storyBeats.speaker: Integration Lead Finn
storyBeats.text: Java 11 introduced a proper HTTP client. Build a client once — it's thread-safe and reusable. Build a request per call. The fluent builder pattern makes it readable. Check the status code before trusting the body.

storyBeats.speaker: GET and POST with HttpClient

learningObjectives: Build a reusable HttpClient and construct GET and POST HttpRequest objects
Send a synchronous request and inspect the status code and body
Set request headers including Content-Type and Authorization
Handle non-200 responses with appropriate conditional logic
commonMistakes: Creating a new HttpClient per request — it's heavy; create one and reuse it
Trusting the response body without checking the status code first
Forgetting Content-Type: application/json header on POST requests — the server may reject the body
Not handling checked exceptions from client.send() — it throws IOException and InterruptedException
assessmentCriteria: Can write a complete GET request using HttpClient and print the response body
Can write a POST request with a JSON string body and correct headers
Can check the status code and branch logic based on 200 vs 404 vs other errors
Can describe what sendAsync returns and why it's preferable in non-blocking contexts
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk through what happens when you call client.send() in Java. What does HttpRequest.newBuilder() do? What does BodyHandlers.ofString() do? Why should you check the status code before using the body?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Simulate calling a REST API using Java's HttpClient. The sandbox has a mock server at http://localhost:8080/api/spells. Write code to:

  1. Make a GET request to /api/spells/1 and print the status code and body
  2. Make a POST request to /api/spells with body {"name":"Icestorm","damage":95} and print the status code
  3. If the GET returns 200, print "Found spell"; if 404, print "Not found"

Note: In this sandbox, the HTTP calls are simulated — the mock methods are provided for you.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From scratch. Write a method String fetchOrDefault(String url, String defaultValue) that makes a GET request to the given URL, returns the response body if status is 200, and returns defaultValue for any other status or exception. Then call it with "https://httpbin.org/status/200" and "https://httpbin.org/status/404" and print both results.

questions.questionHtml: Which Java class (Java 11+) is used to make HTTP requests?
questions.explanationHtml: java.net.http.HttpClient was introduced in Java 11 as the modern, fluent replacement for the older HttpURLConnection. It supports synchronous and asynchronous requests, HTTP/2, and WebSocket.

questions.questionHtml: A developer's POST request to create a resource always returns 400 Bad Request from the server. The URL is correct. What is the most likely cause?
options: The response body has a parse error
The request is missing a required header (e.g. Content-Type: application/json) or the JSON body is malformed
The server does not support POST
The HttpClient should be recreated for each request
questions.correctAnswer: The request is missing a required header (e.g. Content-Type: application/json) or the JSON body is malformed
questions.explanationHtml: 400 Bad Request typically means the server cannot parse or validate the request. Missing Content-Type: application/json causes many servers to reject the body entirely. Also check that the JSON string is well-formed (correctly escaped quotes, valid structure).
